KEY MESSAGE 1...

The pattern shaping up heading into midweek features 
unseasonably strong flow for this close to the summer solstice, 
amid a trough in the east and ridge in the west long wave 
pattern.

Several short wave troughs within the larger long wave trough
over the east travers today through Thursday night. The first
will exit the area this morning, leaving behind scattered
showers over the middle Ohio Valley that will dissipate by
sunrise. A dry day then ensues in a calm before the storms,
although southwest winds do become a bit gusty today amid a 
warmer afternoon.

The second short wave trough drives an unseasonably intense 
surface low pressure center, and then the lower Great Lakes 
tonight into Thursday, with a modest deepening from 990 to 985 
MB along the way. A mid-level jet max of as high as 90 kts is 
forecast within a narrow ribbon of tight height and thermal 
gradients from MT southeastward through WY, and then eastward 
across the midwest and on through PA, and then up through New 
England.

The h85 jet increases to 60 kts tonight across the middle Ohio 
Valley amid tight low level height/pressure gradients, cranking 
h85 theta E values into the 340s K while associated moisture 
flux convergence (moisture transport up to 500 gm/kgs) 
contributes greatly to PW values, which approach two inches 
Thursday atop surface dew points climbing into the low to mid 
70s. After peaking around sunrise Thursday, this strong flow 
decreases steadily during the day on Thursday.

With the help of veering with height of the strong low-level
flow, NAM12 Storm Relative Helicities exceed 500 m2/s2 across
much of the area early Thursday morning amid low LCLs. The unit-
less Significant Tornado Parameter peaking anywhere from 3 west
around 12Z to 1 east around 15Z Thursday suggest a Tornado 
threat, and the Storm Prediction Center Day 1 Outlook has a two 
percent Tornado Risk nudging into the middle Ohio Valley from 
the west. These impressive parameters may be enough to thwart 
non-diurnal timing, and most any thunderstorm in this 
environment is liable to produce or bring down strong to 
damaging wind gusts.

While the NAM12 may be over-zealous with its Severe and
Tornado parameters, even the GFS peaks STP to 1 in the middle
Ohio Valley with the NSHARP algorithm highlighting a Tornado 
threat off of that model as well. The CAMs show somewhat lower
values peaking a bit earlier during the overnight hours tonight,
and a bit farther south.

The flow, strongest northwest in the morning, gradually wanes 
during the day Thursday, but ample low level moisture is likely
to support CAPE increasing to over a KJ/kg amid 0-6 and 0-8 km 
shear in the 40s, even 50s, kts, a damaging wind threat will 
still exist until the cold front crosses from northwest to 
southeast during the late afternoon and evening Thursday.

The Storm Prediction Center has a Marginal to Slight Risk
for Severe Thunderstorms into the middle Ohio Valley in their 
Day 1 outlook, which depicts the overnight/pre-dawn threat, 
with all three hazards, especially wind, nudging in from the 
west. SPC has a Slight Risk for areas southeast of the Ohio
River Thursday, with a Marginal Risk northwest of it, for mainly
a damaging wind gust threat.

The moisture parameters are certainly high enough for an 
Excessive Rainfall Risk even with fast storm motion, especially 
in poor drainage or highly saturated areas and/or repetitive 
storms starting early Thursday and potentially building through 
the day.

Once the front crosses Thursday evening, the third short wave 
trough triggers a wave along it. With moisture feeding into 
southern portions of the area from a southern stream system, 
along and south of the confluence zone between the northern and 
southern stream systems, the risk of excessive rainfall could 
linger across southern portions of the area Thursday night into
Friday morning.

Mirroring the Severe Thunderstorm Risks from SPC, the Weather
Prediction Center edges Marginal to Slight Risks for Excessive
rainfall into the middle Ohio Valley in their Day 1 outlook, 
which depicts the overnight/pre-dawn threat, and then a Marginal
to Slight Risk southeast of the Ohio River Thursday/Thursday 
night. They also depict a Marginal Risk for Excessive rainfall 
clipping our southwest Virginia counties on Friday,

In addition to the thunderstorm and flooding threats mentioned 
above, winds will likely turn gusty ahead of the cold front
tonight, with gusts reaching the 30 to 40 mph range for most
overnight tonight through Thursday morning, with potential for 
wind advisory level gusts in the higher elevations of the 
northeast WV mountains.

KEY MESSAGE 2...

In the wake of the cold front, a high pressure center will  
provide dry weather in time for the start of the weekend. 
Expect near-normal temperatures and lower humidity Friday and 
Saturday, with increasing sunshine from northwest to southeast
on Friday, and then plenty of sunshine for Saturday. Cool
